'to taking' why says 'After to the base form is used, not -ing': false blanket (look forward to + -ing, item vform-004). Say 'ask someone to' is an infinitive, so the verb is base form.

'to played' why: 'After to the verb must be base form' is an unqualified blanket that contradicts look forward to + -ing. Also 'were seen to play' is grammatical but not offered. Giveaway: 'to played' is plainly bad.
'to raised' why uses the same unqualified 'After to ... base form' blanket; restrict to infinitive to. 'to raised' is also a form giveaway.
neither/nor: nearer subject friends, plural; present perfect
'was' why claims the tense does not match 'going to announce'; 'was going to announce' is a valid past form. The real fault is singular was with plural 'prefects'.
verb agrees with nearer subject teacher; "for weeks" needs perfect
singular subject teacher; "together with" ignored; since

'none' why says 'none is used for three or more things': false blanket. 'None of them works' is acceptable standard English, only less precise than 'neither' for two. Fix: make 'none' clearly wrong (e.g. different stem) or drop it as a distractor.
"either ... or" after cannot; "any" cannot precede "my pen"
not all means some were wrong
negative statement, positive tag with she
"everyone" takes they; positive so negative tag
"nothing" is negative, so positive tag "was it"
Giveaway: 'usedn't she' is a rare/odd form, easy to eliminate.
hardly is negative, so positive tag; anyone takes "they"
neither is negative, they + positive did

'But' why says 'But cannot begin a sentence like this': muddled; 'But' can begin sentences. Real fault is that 'But it was very hot, we played outside' is a comma splice with the wrong order of contrast.

'otherwise' why says 'means if not, which does not fit a past event': false ('otherwise' is fine with past events). Real reason: no unwanted alternative is stated; the sentence needs a result link. 'however/nevertheless' are also arguable in a loose reading, but 'therefore' is clearly best.
Giveaway: 'their own selves' is an easy odd-one-out.

'would' why says it cannot express a conclusion from evidence: 'would' can express a probable inference ('the shop would be closed by now'), so 'would' is weakly arguable. 'must' remains the best key; make the distractor clearly wrong or soften the why.
needn't: no need given sunny forecast
Giveaway: 'would not have being' is a form giveaway.
if only + had had for past regret
Stem 'If only I had had more time ..., I would have finished' mixes a wish ('If only') with a result clause; unnatural. Key 'had had' is right. Suggest 'If I ____ more time yesterday'.
Filled sentence 'pick up us' is ungrammatical; with a pronoun it must be 'pick us up'. Change stem (e.g. 'pick up the pupils') or object.
'called for' why is muddled ('a picnic that has happened'); say it means 'require/demand' and 'The picnic was called for' makes no sense.
switch off when leaving the room (on would not fit context)
'broke down' why ('a fire does not stop working when it starts') is a nonsensical explanation; rewrite as 'means stopped working or collapsed; a fire that begins is not stopping'.
run out of = have none left
keep down your voice = make it quieter
Natural order is 'keep your voice down'; 'keep down your voice' is acceptable but awkward. Consider rewording the stem.
put out a fire = extinguish it
'drop by at my house' is non-standard; 'drop by my house' or 'drop in at my house'. Distractor 'stay up' is not a drop- phrase, a mild giveaway.
come down with = catch an illness
make up = reconcile after a quarrel
crack down on = act strictly against
see through a lie = detect it
take up an offer = accept it
Filled sentence 'let down you' is ungrammatical; needs 'let you down'. Fix stem (e.g. 'let ___ down' or use 'her/a friend' object).
roll out a product = launch gradually
let the cat out of the bag = reveal a secret by accident
up to his eyes in work = very busy
Standard idiom is 'up to his eyes IN work', not 'with'; as written the keyed phrase is wrong. Change 'with work' to 'in work'.

beating around the bush = avoiding the point
barking up the wrong tree = accusing the wrong person
jump on the bandwagon = follow a trend
Giveaway: 'was soon ___' needs a participle/adjective; the other three options are past-tense verb phrases and are grammatically impossible.

Filled sentence 'take with a pinch of salt what he says' is unnatural; standard is 'take what he says with a pinch of salt'. Restructure the stem.

Over-broad rule: 'the if clause cannot contain would' is false (polite 'if you would...'). Say it is wrong because an unreal past condition takes the past perfect.

No context says the homework is still finished; 'has finished' is acceptable when the report is made while still relevant. Add a '(it was finished then)' cue or a time marker that forces backshift.

Reporting 'has she finished' is possible if the project is still the topic; add context. Distractor 'if she has finished' is only wrong by assumption. 'if she finished' is also acceptable but not offered.
'today' is acceptable if the report is made on Monday itself; stem gives no cue that the report is made later. Add 'Later, ...' or similar.
Present perfect to had bought; yesterday to the day before.

Present perfect backshifts to had lived.
Backshift is optional when still true; if Mr Goh still lives there, 'has lived' is fine. Add context such as '(He moved away this year.)'.
Backshift: had been waiting, statement order.
